# Solving the model

## Overview
`ems_solve()` solves the constrained optimization problem according to a range of runtime configuration options.
In order to solve, a teems Docker [image](https://github.com/teemsphere/teems-solver) must be prebuilt.
Singularity, accuracy, and error checks are carried out following a successful run.
By default, solver outputs are automatically parsed into structured R objects via [`ems_compose()`](compose.qmd).

## Arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `cmf_path` | | Path to the CMF file generated by [`ems_deploy()`](deploy.qmd) |
| `solution_method` | `"Johansen"` | Solution method (see below) |
| `matrix_method` | `"LU"` | Matrix solution method (see below); [`ems_probe()`](#recommended) recommends the one to use |
| `n_subintervals` | `1L` | Number of subintervals for the applied shock. More subintervals may alleviate accuracy issues stemming from large shock magnitudes |
| `steps` | `c(2L, 4L, 8L)` | Strictly increasing vector of three step counts for the `"Gragg"` and `"Euler"` methods. For `"Gragg"` all three must additionally be even (required by the method's extrapolation theory; Pearson 1991); `"Euler"` has no parity requirement. The Runge-Kutta methods take a single step count instead (e.g. `steps = 8L`) |
| `adaptive` | `"no"` | Adaptive step-size control for the embedded Runge-Kutta methods (`"BoSha32"`, `"DoPri54"`): `"yes"` redoes steps whose worst accuracy metric exceeds `eps_tolerance` (or on which a percentage-change variable crosses `-100%`) with a smaller step size and adjusts the next step size after every accepted step; `"accuracy-only"` acts on the accuracy metric alone |
| `eps_tolerance` | `0.01` | Per-step accuracy-metric bound targeted by `adaptive` control. The default is the measured optimum (four correct digits on 92-96% of elements at a third of the factorizations, see below); `0.1` is a cheaper exploratory setting. Values below `0.005` are hard to achieve numerically |
| `n_tasks` | `1L` | Number of tasks to run in parallel. Must be `1L` if `matrix_method` is `"LU"` |
| `n_threads` | `1L` | OpenMP threads per task |
| `suppress_outputs` | `FALSE` | When `TRUE`, solver outputs are not automatically parsed with [`ems_compose()`](compose.qmd) |
| `verbosity` | `1L` | Solver log detail: `0` errors, warnings and the accuracy summary; `1` adds phase progress and timings; `2` adds per-rank and per-block detail |
| `assertions` | `"fatal"` | Severity of TAB `Assertion` failures (GEMPACK 25.3): `"fatal"`, `"warn"` or `"off"` |
| `range_test_initial` | `"warn"` | Severity of declared-range violations (e.g. `(ge 0)`) on initial values (GEMPACK `range test initial values`; its `yes`/`warn`/`no` are `"fatal"`/`"warn"`/`"off"`) |
| `range_test_updated` | `"warn"` | As `range_test_initial`, for updated values |
| `postsim` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` skips the TAB's `PostSim` sections |
| `terminal_run` | `FALSE` | When `TRUE`, exits without running the solver, allowing the user to close R and run from the terminal |
| `...` | | Additional named solver arguments: the Runge-Kutta step controls (`max_retries`, `retry_adjust`), the MA48 workspace initial guesses (`laA`, `laD`, `laDi` — normally left unset: the solver sizes its workspace automatically, growing it as needed and warm-starting repeat runs from the recorded `la_used` in `sol.stats.json`) and the expert solver flags (`inmemory` — value arrays and block factors resident in memory, the solver's default for every method except `"NDBBD"` — `fastrefac`, `gpzerodivide`, `cntl_3`, `cntl_6`, `nsbbdblocks`, `withmc66`, `smllthreads`, `tempdir`, `nowrites`, `condest`, e.g. `smllthreads = 2L`). Unknown names are an error, never a silently ignored flag |

## Basic usage

```r
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Johansen",
  matrix_method = "LU"
)
```

## Solution methods

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `"Johansen"` | Fast one-step approximation. Should only be used as a rough approximation due to handling of nonlinear equations. See [GEMPACK manual](https://www.copsmodels.com/gpmanual.htm#gpd1.2.13) |
| `"Gragg"` | Gragg's method (the smoothed modified midpoint method; Pearson 1991): the shock is applied over multiple linearized passes whose solutions are combined by Richardson extrapolation for improved accuracy. The `steps` parameter controls the per-pass step counts. See [GEMPACK manual](https://www.copsmodels.com/gpmanual.htm#gpd3.12.2) |
| `"Euler"` | The forward Euler method with the same three-solution Richardson extrapolation. Converges more slowly than `"Gragg"` (one order gained per extrapolation solution instead of two) but is the most robust multistep choice: each step uses only the current state, so it tolerates variables approaching asymptotes and severe shocks — including exact `-100%` shocks — where the midpoint family can become unstable. See [GEMPACK manual](https://www.copsmodels.com/gpmanual.htm#gpd3.12.2) |
| `"RK2"`, `"Heun"`, `"RK4"` | Explicit Runge-Kutta methods (the midpoint rule, Heun's explicit trapezoid rule, and the classic fourth-order method; Schiffmann 2022). A single solution is computed with one step count, no Richardson extrapolation, each step built from 2, 2 or 4 staged linear solves. `"Heun"` and `"RK2"` cost the same; Heun is strong-stability-preserving, the midpoint rule is not. `"RK4"` with a handful of steps is the cheapest method that reaches four correct digits on large shocks in TEEMS's own measurements. Stages are combined in log-levels by default (see `chart` in [`ems_RK()`]), so a percentage-change variable cannot reach `-100%` at any stage |
| `"BoSha32"`, `"DoPri54"` | Embedded Runge-Kutta pairs (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2), 4 stages; Dormand-Prince 5(4), 7 stages; both first-same-as-last, so an accepted step costs 3 or 6 new solves). Alongside the solution they accumulate a per-element error estimate, returned as the `error_estimate` column by [`ems_compose()`] and written beside the solution as `sol.est`. Treat it as an indicator of the least-settled elements: in TEEMS's measurements at scale it under-reads the true error on a third to a half of the elements, so it is not an upper bound. With `adaptive = "yes"` the step size is controlled against `eps_tolerance` and a step is redone when the estimate, a coefficient range test, an assertion or (percent chart only) a `-100%` crossing fails; use the accuracy ladders (repeat the run with tighter `eps_tolerance` or more `steps`) when a bound is needed |

## Matrix methods
Increase `n_tasks` to take advantage of parallel matrix solution methods. Nothing is chosen for you: the run is exactly the arguments given, so it is reproducible from its record on any machine, and a bare `ems_solve(cmf_path)` runs `"LU"` on one task and one thread, which is correct for every model and slow for a large intertemporal one. [`ems_probe()`](#recommended) makes the choice explicit.
<!-- Add links to matrix method papers -->
| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `"LU"` | Standard LU decomposition. The most robust and potentially slowest for large models. `n_tasks` must be `1L`. Works with both static and dynamic models |
| `"DBBD"` | Doubly bordered block diagonal. Parallel matrix solution method for static models only. Potentially faster than `"LU"` although less robust |
| `"SBBD"` | Singly bordered block diagonal. Parallel matrix solution method for intertemporal models only. Potentially faster than `"LU"` although less robust |
| `"NDBBD"` | Nested doubly bordered block diagonal. Parallel matrix solution method for large intertemporal models with many timesteps only |

## Multi-step solution

For greater accuracy, use the Gragg method with subintervals:
```r
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Gragg",
  matrix_method = "LU",
  n_subintervals = 2,
  steps = c(2, 4, 8)
)
```

Or an adaptive embedded Runge-Kutta run, which controls its own step
sizes against `eps_tolerance` and reports a per-element error
estimate (subintervals do not apply — the controller replaces them).
On large shocks measured against 32-step references (2026-09), adaptive
`"DoPri54"` at `eps_tolerance = 0.01` reaches the accuracy of `"Gragg"`
with four subintervals for about half the factorizations, and the
accuracy of the previous driver for about a third; single-subinterval
`"Gragg"` is not a solution on such shocks, and `"RK4"` with four steps
is the cheapest route to three to four correct digits. `eps_tolerance =
0.1` is loose now that only percentage-change variables steer the step
(see `scope` in [`ems_RK()`]); the comparison is in the developer notes
(`rk_comparison.md`):
```r
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "DoPri54",
  matrix_method = "LU",
  steps = 4,
  adaptive = "yes",
  eps_tolerance = 0.01
)
outputs$dat$qgdp$error_estimate
```

## Memory parameters

`laA`, `laD` and `laDi` size the MA48 factorization workspaces, as a percentage of the matrix's non-zero count. They are only initial guesses: when a factorization runs out of workspace the solver grows it and retries automatically, notes the new size in the log ("MA48 workspace grown from ... to ..."), and records what it settled on as `la_used` in `sol.stats.json`. Normally you never set them.

- `laA` applies to `"LU"` and `"SBBD"` methods
- `laD` applies to `"DBBD"` and `"NDBBD"` methods
- `laDi` applies to the `"NDBBD"` method only

Setting one is worth doing only to skip that discovery: each growth costs a failed factorization, so a run whose log shows growth will start faster next time if seeded at the recorded `la_used`. Oversizing is close to free — the extra workspace is mostly untouched pages — so seed generously rather than tightly.

```r
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Johansen",
  matrix_method = "LU",
  laA = 500L
)
```

### The workspace ceiling

The HSL kernels are built with 32-bit integers, so a single MA48 workspace cannot exceed 2,147,483,647 elements no matter what you pass. A system whose factorization needs more than that aborts with

```
Error: factorizing <system> needs a larger MA48 workspace than the
2147483647-element limit of the 32-bit HSL build ...
```

This is a limit on one *sequential* factorization, not on the model. The remedies are to split the factorization across blocks with a bordered method (`matrix_method = "SBBD"` or `"DBBD"`), to condense the model so the solved system is smaller, or to reduce its dimensions. Raising `laA` further cannot help, and the solver will say so rather than retrying.

## Checking solve quality

If a model solves but the results look implausible — percent changes orders of magnitude too large, or accuracy figures that will not settle — the cause may be numerical rather than structural. `ems_probe()` catches wrong closures (variables nothing determines, equations that determine the same variable twice), but a model can be structurally perfect and still be numerically degenerate, typically when the closure depends on base-data flows that are very close to zero.

`condest = TRUE` measures every linear solve and reports it:

```r
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Gragg",
  matrix_method = "LU",
  condest = TRUE
)
```

Each solve logs a backward error (how faithfully the system was solved) and the scaled condition numbers `kappa_w1`/`kappa_w2` (how sensitive the answer is to the data). Run maxima are recorded in `sol.stats.json` and appear in the model diagnostics. Read `kappa_w2`: values around `1e8`–`1e9` are ordinary for CGE Jacobians, while values approaching `1e15` trigger a warning that the system is numerically near-singular and its solutions are unreliable — the signal to look for near-zero flows your closure depends on, or to rerun with `precision = "f64"`.

The diagnostic never changes results — solutions are identical with it on or off — and it costs a few percent of solve time. It applies to the `"LU"` matrix method (the bordered methods warn and ignore it), and reports nothing for a zero shock, where there is nothing to measure.

## Memory use

Every run records how much memory it held. After each phase (variable calculation, variable broadcast, matrix preparation, calculation and assembly), after each step and after the solve, the solver logs a `memory:` line with the resident set of the largest rank and the total over all ranks, plus the high-water mark so far:

```
memory: after matrix assembly, resident 5.12 GB max per rank, 18.40 GB over 4 rank(s); high-water 5.20 GB max, 18.60 GB sum
```

The same numbers are recorded per phase as `rss_gb` in `sol.stats.json` and summarised in the model diagnostics. Read the two columns differently: the *max* is what one rank needs, so it decides whether a run fits a host at a given rank count; the *sum* is what the job holds in total, and since the value tables are replicated on every rank the sum grows with the rank count. When a large run is close to the machine's memory, the phase with the peak says where the memory goes, and fewer ranks usually help before a different matrix method does.

Under `"NDBBD"` memory also grows with the thread count: four regions of the solve hold per-thread working sets sized by the interface between periods (the dense interface product, the interface staged at `laDi` percent, and a chain block's factors read back from scratch), so a 234-million-equation run measured 62 GB plus 2.9 GB per thread on one rank. The solver sizes each region's per-thread footprint from the deployed structure before its threads start and lowers the thread count so that the ranks on the host fit within 0.8 of the memory still available (the container's memory limit is honoured). The choice is logged as an `ndbbd threads:` line with the per-thread breakdown and recorded as `ndbbd_threads` in `sol.stats.json`; it changes only the wall time, never the solution.

### The memory model and the pre-solve check

Before a run starts, teems-R estimates its peak memory and compares it with the container's memory (Docker Desktop's Resources setting on a laptop, the cgroup limit or the machine's memory elsewhere; read once per session from inside the image). The estimate is per *plain-equivalent* equation, the solved system plus the backsolved elements, because condensation cuts the equation count about twentyfold but not the peak memory (the value tables follow the data):

| Method | Peak memory, kB per plain-equivalent equation | Measured on |
|---|---|---|
| `"LU"` | 0.90 (1.2 × that when condensed) | 0.58-0.70 to 3.8 million equations, 0.84-0.90 at 7.7 million |
| `"DBBD"` | 0.85 + 0.27 per task (1.55 × that when condensed) | 346 thousand to 7.7 million; matches the binding 12 GB cell within 3 %, over-predicts smaller systems by up to a quarter |
| `"SBBD"` | 0.36 + 0.02 per task | 1.3 to 8.9 million; extrapolates to 21.9 million within 15 % |
| `"NDBBD"` | 0.15 per task + 0.05 | replicated tables at 234 million equations (34.7 GB on one rank) plus the local matrix share; thread working sets are budgeted by the solver |

A run whose estimate exceeds the container's memory by more than the model's error band (20 %) is refused by name before it starts, with the estimate, the limit and the remedies (a coarser aggregation, condensation, a higher Docker Desktop memory limit, fewer tasks under `"DBBD"`, `"NDBBD"` at one task for an intertemporal model, or a larger host); a run inside the band is warned about. The same estimates keep `ems_probe()` from recommending `"DBBD"` where it would not fit and make it recommend `"NDBBD"` for an intertemporal model where `"SBBD"` would not. The estimate and the verdict are written to `model_diagnostics.txt`.

Two solves of the same deployment give byte-identical solutions with `"LU"`, `"SBBD"` and `"NDBBD"` at any thread count. With `"DBBD"` the border contributions of the diagonal blocks are accumulated in whatever order the threads finish, so at `n_threads` above 1 repeated runs differ at the floating-point rounding level (of the order of 1e-10 relative on well-determined elements, sign flips on numerical zeros; a multi-step extrapolation on a poorly conditioned aggregation can amplify this to a few digits on the least-determined elements). Use `n_threads = 1L` with `"DBBD"` when byte-for-byte reproducibility matters.

## Parallel solving

For models that support parallel matrix methods, increase `n_tasks`:
```r
outputs <- ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Johansen",
  matrix_method = "SBBD",
  n_tasks = 4
)
```

### Recommended method and resources {#recommended}

`ems_probe()` measures the deployed system's structure (chain dimension, block partition, border), reads the deploy metadata (size, regions, condensation) and the container's cores and memory, and prints a recommendation with its evidence, the memory estimate and the call to paste:

```r
probe <- ems_probe(cmf_path)
#> recommended for 8 cores, 12.0 GB (this container): "SBBD", 3 tasks x 2 threads
#>   evidence: 4,540,000 equations, chain alltime (3 blocks), ...
#>   ems_solve(cmf_path, matrix_method = "SBBD", n_tasks = 3, n_threads = 2)
```

Pass `cores` and `memory` (GB) to get the recommendation for a machine you are not on. The rules were measured on a 12 GB laptop profile with 4 and 8 cores and on a 32-core box (developer notes `hpc_auto_plan.md`, section 3.5):

| Model | Method | Tasks | Threads | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| intertemporal | `"SBBD"` | `min(8, cores, time steps)` | the remaining cores per task, at most 8 | fastest at every measured size (2.4 to 230 million equations); ranks beat threads at every fixed core count and each doubling past four buys at most 11 % |
| intertemporal, SBBD too big for the memory | `"NDBBD"` | 1 | every core | the replicated tables are held once; the solver budgets the threads of each region from their memory footprint |
| static, uncondensed, with a usable partition | `"DBBD"` | 2 on a laptop (8 cores or fewer); `cores / 4`, at most 8, on a bigger host; fewer where the memory model says so | the remaining cores per task, at most 8 | faster than LU at every rung from 346 thousand to 7.7 million equations; wall is flat from two tasks at laptop sizes while each task costs 0.27 kB per equation |
| static, condensed (the vetted GTAP models) | `"LU"` below about 120 thousand condensed equations (70 thousand under Johansen), `"DBBD"` above if its estimate fits | 1 / as above | up to 8 | condensed LU speeds up 29-81 % with threads and wins to that size; condensed DBBD gets slower with more tasks |

The probe costs one pre-solve pipeline plus the matching: seconds on condensed systems, a few times a Johansen solve on intertemporal ones, and more than the solve itself on uncondensed static systems above a few million equations, so run it once per deployment. Scratch-backed runs (`"NDBBD"`, `inmemory = FALSE`) get their scratch directory inside the container filesystem (`tempdir = "/tmp"` unless given), because docker's `/dev/shm` is 64 MB by default.

### Running on a laptop

Docker Desktop hands the solver a Linux VM with the memory and CPUs set under Settings > Resources; on a 16 GB laptop set the memory to 12 GB (8 GB leaves room for little beyond the vetted models at a medium aggregation). What fits in 12 GB, measured on that profile with Gragg 2-4-8: every intertemporal deployment to about 20 million equations under `"SBBD"` (8.9 million equations peak at 4.5 GB); uncondensed static systems to 7.7 million equations under `"DBBD"` at two tasks (10.8-11.2 GB) or `"LU"` (6.5 GB Johansen); condensed static systems to about 140 thousand condensed equations under `"DBBD"` at two tasks (6.4 GB) and to 230 thousand under threaded `"LU"` (6 GB). The vetted GTAP models at a medium aggregation condense to 25-200 thousand equations and solve in seconds to minutes; run `ems_probe(cmf_path)` once per deployment for the method and resources to use, and the "fits" verdict of any solve is in its `model_diagnostics.txt`. `-fastrefac` and `inmemory = FALSE` are not laptop levers: the first is slower on 1.4-3.8 million-equation systems and the second saves no memory.

### Concurrent runs

Several model runs can solve at the same time, one deploy directory each.
The directory is set by the `tempdir` option, so give every run its own before deploying it:

```r
for (case in c("johansen", "gragg")) {
  ems_option_set(tempdir = file.path("~/runs", case))
  dat <- ems_data(dat_input, par_input, set_input, REG = "big3", ACTS = "macro_sector")
  cmf <- ems_deploy(dat, model, shock)
  # solve each cmf in its own process
}
```

Runs separated this way do not touch each other: each has its own solver scratch files, its own solution binaries and its own log.

Two solves in one deploy directory are not supported and the second is refused by name.
They would share the solver's scratch files, which are named from the MPI rank alone, and the solution binaries and CSV outputs the CMF names, so both runs would be corrupted rather than one.
A run that is interrupted can leave its claim behind, in which case the message names the `.solve_lock` directory to remove.

## Terminal mode

For long-running models, `terminal_run` allows the user to close any R IDE prior to running from the terminal:
```r
ems_solve(
  cmf_path = cmf_path,
  solution_method = "Johansen",
  matrix_method = "LU",
  terminal_run = TRUE
)
```

## Solving in-situ

`solve_in_situ()` calls the [teems-solver](https://github.com/teemsphere/teems-solver) directly with user-supplied input files, bypassing the [`ems_data()`](data_load.qmd) / [`ems_model()`](model_load.qmd) / [`ems_deploy()`](deploy.qmd) pipeline.
The model file will be parsed but all input files must be provided in their final form.
No checks or modifications are applied to input files.

This function is intended for users who wish to use the teems solver with pre-prepared input files, or in combination with the standard pipeline by reusing the files written to disk by [`ems_deploy()`](deploy.qmd).
If all input files already reside in `model_dir`, no copying is performed; otherwise files are copied into `model_dir` before solving.

### Arguments

| Argument | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `...` | | Named arguments corresponding to input files necessary for an in-situ model run. Names must correspond to "File" statements within the model Tablo file. Values correspond to file paths where these files are found |
| `model_dir` | | Base directory where input files will be copied if not already present, and model outputs will be written |
| `model_file` | | Path to the model Tablo (.tab) file |
| `closure_file` | | Path to the closure (.cls) file |
| `shock_file` | | Path to the shock (.shf) file |
| `solution_method` | `"Johansen"` | Solution method: `"Johansen"`, `"Gragg"`, `"Euler"`, `"RK2"`, `"RK4"`, `"BoSha32"`, or `"DoPri54"` |
| `matrix_method` | `"LU"` | Matrix solution method: `"LU"`, `"DBBD"`, `"SBBD"`, or `"NDBBD"` |
| `n_subintervals` | `1L` | Number of subintervals for the applied shock |
| `steps` | `c(2L, 4L, 8L)` | Vector of steps for the Gragg method |
| `n_tasks` | `1L` | Number of tasks to run in parallel. Must be `1L` if `matrix_method` is `"LU"` |
| `suppress_outputs` | `FALSE` | When `TRUE`, returns the CMF file path instead of parsed outputs |
| `terminal_run` | `FALSE` | When `TRUE`, exits without running the solver |
| `solver_args` | `NULL` | Named list of the additional solver arguments `ems_solve()` accepts through `...` (the MA48 workspace initial guesses and the expert solver flags, e.g. `list(smllthreads = 2L)`); a list because the in-situ `...` carries the input files |

### Input files

All model-declared input files as well as `model_file`, `closure_file`, and `shock_file` are required.
Input files are passed as named arguments via `...`, where each name must correspond to a "File" statement in the model Tablo file.
For GTAP-RE, the Tablo file declares:

```
File GTAPDATA # base data file;
File GTAPINT  # intertemporal data file;
File GTAPPARM # parameter file;
File GTAPSETS # set file;
```

These names are then used as the named arguments to `solve_in_situ()`.
```r
solve_in_situ(
  GTAPDATA = file.path(write_dir, "teems", "GTAPDATA.txt"),
  GTAPINT = file.path(write_dir, "teems", "GTAPINT.txt"),
  GTAPPARM = file.path(write_dir, "teems", "GTAPPARM.txt"),
  GTAPSETS = file.path(write_dir, "teems", "GTAPSETS.txt"),
  model_dir = "~/in_situ_run/",
  model_file = "GTAP-RE.tab",
  closure_file = "GTAP-RE.cls",
  shock_file = "a_shock_file.shf",
  solution_method = "Gragg",
  matrix_method = "SBBD",
  n_subintervals = 1L,
  n_tasks = 1L
)
```

The model file is processed exactly as `ems_model()` processes it, so in-TAB `Omit`, `Substitute`, and `Backsolve` statements apply.
Pass `ignore_condense = TRUE` when the closure and shock files were produced from a model loaded with `ems_model(..., ignore_condense = TRUE)`, otherwise the closure will name variables the condensed model no longer carries.

### Output modes

By default, `solve_in_situ()` returns a tibble containing model output variables and coefficients.
If `suppress_outputs = TRUE`, the function returns the CMF file path instead, which can be passed to [`ems_compose()`](compose.qmd) for manual parsing.
